issues.legal_issue: An institution may be declared a Sikh Gurdwara under the statutory test only when it was established for use by Sikhs for public worship and was used for that worship by Sikhs before and at the time of the relevant petition.
material_facts: The institution was founded by an Udasi Faqir, and succession to its mahant’s office was from Guru to Chela.
The evidence did not establish that the institution was founded for use by Sikhs for public worship.
The institution came to be used for reading or worship of Granth Sahib by Sikhs, alongside its use by Udasis, and later records described it as a Gurdwara.
The Tribunal declared the institution a Sikh Gurdwara, but the High Court set that declaration aside.
issues.conclusion: The institution could not be declared a Sikh Gurdwara because it was not shown to have been established for use by Sikhs for public worship; later Sikh worship or descriptions in records did not cure that failure.
issues.legal_principle: Section 16(2)(iii) of the Sikh Gurdwaras Act, 1925 requires both establishment for use by Sikhs for public worship and use for that worship by Sikhs before and at the time of the petition; the conjunctive wording makes the conditions cumulative. The Court approved Gurmukh Singh v. Risaldar Deva Singh for this interpretation. Later use or revenue-record descriptions do not establish the purpose for which the institution was founded.

predicates.gurdwara_status_proceeding: The proceeding asks whether an institution qualifies for recognition as a Sikh Gurdwara.
predicates.established_for_sikh_public_worship: The institution was established for use by Sikhs for public worship.
predicates.used_for_sikh_public_worship_at_required: Sikhs used the institution for public worship both before and when the relevant petition was presented.

issues.definition: In a proceeding about Gurdwara status, failure of either the establishment condition or the required-use condition results in the institution not qualifying as a Sikh Gurdwara.

issues.legal_issue: Veneration or reading of Sikh scriptures at an institution does not, by itself, establish that the institution is a Sikh Gurdwara when the institution’s character is associated with the independent Udasi sect.
material_facts: The institution was founded by an Udasi Faqir, and its mahant succession was from Guru to Chela.
The institution was described in records as a Dera of the Udasi Bhekh and was used by Udasis as well as Sikhs.
Granth Sahib was read or venerated at the institution, but the evidence did not show that it had been established for Sikh public worship.
issues.conclusion: The veneration or reading of Granth Sahib was not decisive of the institution’s character and did not establish that it was a Sikh Gurdwara.
issues.legal_principle: The Court treated Udasis as an independent sect that also venerates Sikh scriptures. It relied on Hem Singh v. Basant Das, Mahant Dharam Dass v. State of Punjab, and Pritam Dass Mahant v. Shiromani Gurdwara Prabandhak Committee in explaining why scripture veneration alone does not determine an institution’s character.

predicates.institution_character_proceeding: The proceeding concerns the religious character of an institution.
predicates.udasi_affiliation: The institution is associated with the Udasi sect through its founder, management, succession, or identity.
predicates.sikh_scriptures_venerated: Sikh scriptures are read or venerated at the institution.

issues.definition: When an institution-character proceeding concerns an Udasi-associated institution where Sikh scriptures are venerated, that veneration alone does not establish Sikh Gurdwara status.
